issues.label: Subject-matter jurisdiction proper
issues.why: The court must confirm it has jurisdiction under the Juvenile Code to hear child-protective proceedings and termination.

issues.label: Personal jurisdiction over respondent
issues.why: The court must ensure respondent was properly served/noticed and is subject to the court’s authority.

issues.label: Proper venue
issues.why: The court must verify the case was filed in the correct county/court under applicable venue rules.

issues.label: Standing/authority of DHHS
issues.why: DHHS must have statutory authority to file the petition and seek the specific relief requested.

issues.label: Petition legal sufficiency
issues.why: The petition must allege facts that, if proven, support jurisdiction and the requested termination grounds.

issues.label: Adequate notice of allegations
issues.why: Due process requires respondent receive clear notice of the claims and statutory grounds pursued.

issues.label: Appointment of counsel requirements
issues.why: The court must ensure respondent’s right to appointed counsel (if eligible) and timely representation was honored.

issues.label: Interpreter/disability accommodations
issues.why: The court must provide any required language or disability accommodations to ensure meaningful participation.

issues.label: Conflicts of interest checked
issues.why: The court must ensure counsel/participants have no disqualifying conflicts affecting fairness.

issues.label: Guardian ad litem/attorney for child
issues.why: The court must determine whether the child requires counsel/representation and ensure proper appointment if mandated.

issues.label: Indian Child Welfare Act inquiry
issues.why: The court must inquire whether ICWA/MIFPA applies and, if so, follow heightened notice and proof standards.

issues.label: Emergency/removal criteria met
issues.why: Any removal/exclusion from respondent’s care must satisfy statutory criteria and be supported by sufficient evidence.

issues.label: Reasonable efforts applicability
issues.why: The court must decide whether DHHS had to make reasonable reunification efforts or whether an exception applies.

issues.label: Aggravated-circumstances exception
issues.why: Sexual abuse may relieve DHHS of reunification efforts; the court must make and support that determination.

issues.label: Preliminary hearing procedures
issues.why: The court must ensure proper procedure and evidentiary basis for authorization and interim orders.

issues.label: No-contact/suspension standards
issues.why: Suspending parenting time must be justified by risk findings and comply with statutory requirements.

issues.label: Adjudication adequacy
issues.why: Jurisdiction must be established by legally sufficient proof at adjudication (or plea) before disposition/termination.

issues.label: Adjudication burden of proof
issues.why: The court must apply the correct burden (preponderance) for jurisdictional findings.

issues.label: Adjudication evidence admissibility
issues.why: The court must admit only competent evidence under the correct evidentiary rules for adjudication.

issues.label: Credibility determinations supported
issues.why: When findings hinge on witness credibility (child disclosures, SANE, respondent), the court must resolve and explain it.

issues.label: Bench-trial findings required
issues.why: The court must make specific findings of fact and conclusions of law sufficient for appellate review.

issues.label: Initial disposition termination permitted
issues.why: The court must confirm termination at initial disposition is procedurally authorized and prerequisites are satisfied.

issues.label: Bifurcation/combined hearing fairness
issues.why: Combining disposition and termination must not violate due process or statutory sequencing.

issues.label: Timing/adjournments due process
issues.why: Two-day hearing spread months apart must still provide fair opportunity to present evidence and respond.

issues.label: Application of correct standards
issues.why: The court must apply clear-and-convincing evidence for statutory grounds and preponderance for best interests.

issues.label: Ground (b)(i) elements met
issues.why: The court must determine whether respondent caused physical injury or sexual abuse and whether there is a likelihood of future injury/abuse if returned.

issues.label: Sexual abuse definition satisfied
issues.why: The court must decide whether the bathing/genital touching constitutes “sexual abuse” within the statute and case law.

issues.label: Causation attributable to respondent
issues.why: For (b)(i), the court must find the injury/abuse was caused by the parent (not merely suspected or by another).

issues.label: Likelihood of future harm
issues.why: Termination under (b)(i) requires a supported finding that future harm is likely if the child is in respondent’s care.

issues.label: Ground (k)(ii) elements met
issues.why: The court must determine whether respondent committed (or attempted) criminal sexual conduct involving penetration as required by (k)(ii).

issues.label: Penetration proof sufficiency
issues.why: If (k)(ii) requires penetration, the court must assess whether evidence shows intrusion, however slight, as legally defined.

issues.label: Attempt theory support
issues.why: If relying on “attempt,” the court must find intent and an overt act beyond preparation under the relevant standard.

issues.label: Need for criminal conviction
issues.why: The court must recognize termination grounds can be proven without a criminal conviction and apply the correct approach.

issues.label: Alternative statutory grounds
issues.why: If multiple grounds are alleged, the court must analyze each and recognize only one proven ground is necessary.

issues.label: Hearsay exceptions for child statements
issues.why: The court must determine whether JS’s out-of-court disclosures (to SANE/investigators/mother) are admissible under applicable exceptions.

issues.label: Medical-treatment hearsay exception
issues.why: Statements to the SANE may be admissible for diagnosis/treatment; the court must apply the correct test.

issues.label: Tender-years/child declarant rules
issues.why: If relying on child statements, the court must comply with any statutory/constitutional reliability requirements for young children.

issues.label: Confrontation clause in civil case
issues.why: The court must address any due process limits on reliance on testimonial hearsay even though Confrontation Clause is criminal.

issues.label: Expert testimony foundation
issues.why: The SANE’s opinions must meet admissibility requirements (qualification, reliable basis, proper scope).

issues.label: Relevance vs unfair prejudice
issues.why: Evidence like respondent’s attraction to the half-sister must be weighed for relevance and unfair prejudice under evidentiary rules.

issues.label: Character/propensity evidence limits
issues.why: The court must consider whether and how sexual-interest evidence is admissible without improper propensity reasoning.

issues.label: UTI evidence probative value
issues.why: The court must evaluate what a UTI does or does not show about sexual abuse and avoid overinference.

issues.label: Behavioral-change evidence weight
issues.why: Night terrors/refusal to visit are circumstantial; the court must assess weight and alternative explanations.

issues.label: Respondent admissions interpretation
issues.why: The court must decide whether admitted genital touching supports an inference of sexual intent or abuse.

issues.label: Intent/sexual purpose requirement
issues.why: If the legal definition of abuse/CSC requires sexual purpose, the court must determine intent from the record.

issues.label: Accidental/innocent touching defense
issues.why: The court must address respondent’s explanation (hygiene/accidents) and decide whether it negates statutory elements.

issues.label: Parental fitness and capacity
issues.why: The court must consider respondent’s ability to provide safe care, supervision, and boundaries.

issues.label: Protective capacity of mother
issues.why: Because JS remained with mother, the court must consider whether safety can be ensured without terminating respondent’s rights.

issues.label: Less restrictive alternatives
issues.why: The court must consider whether orders short of termination (supervised contact/no-contact, services) could protect JS.

issues.label: Parenting time feasibility
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether any safe parenting time could occur and what conditions would be required.

issues.label: Relative placement considerations
issues.why: If a relative placement is relevant/available, the court must consider how it affects best interests and permanency.

issues.label: Child’s placement stability
issues.why: Best interests analysis must address stability and continuity in JS’s current placement with her mother.

issues.label: Bond with respondent
issues.why: The court must weigh evidence of a bond against safety risks and potential trauma.

issues.label: Child’s age and vulnerability
issues.why: JS’s young age increases risk and affects best-interest and safety analysis.

issues.label: Trauma and therapeutic needs
issues.why: The court must consider the impact of alleged abuse, need for counseling, and whether respondent impedes healing.

issues.label: Permanency and finality
issues.why: The court must consider JS’s need for permanency and whether termination advances it given mother’s custody.

issues.label: Effect of termination when noncustodial
issues.why: Because respondent is noncustodial, the court must consider whether termination is necessary to achieve safety and stability.

issues.label: Future contact risk assessment
issues.why: The court must assess risk posed by respondent’s potential access (including through mother/others) absent termination.

issues.label: Protective orders enforceability
issues.why: If considering non-termination options, the court must consider enforceability and compliance likelihood.

issues.label: Respondent’s insight/remorse
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether respondent recognizes boundaries/risk, affecting likelihood of future harm.

issues.label: Respondent’s credibility at disposition
issues.why: Termination rests on factual findings; the court must decide credibility of respondent and siblings’ testimony.

issues.label: Sibling witnesses relevance
issues.why: The court must assess whether siblings’ bond testimony meaningfully rebuts abuse findings or is speculative.

issues.label: Domestic/household environment
issues.why: The court must consider any home environment factors that affect the ability to keep JS safe around respondent.

issues.label: Sexualized statements about half-sister
issues.why: The court must decide what weight to give respondent’s sexual attraction to a minor in assessing risk to JS.

issues.label: Half-sister’s status/age changes
issues.why: The court must consider any relevance of the half-sister turning 18 to risk assessment and evidentiary inferences.

issues.label: Services and treatment suitability
issues.why: If services are considered, the court must evaluate whether sexual-abuse-related services are appropriate or futile.

issues.label: Reasonable efforts findings on record
issues.why: If efforts were required or excused, the court must make explicit findings to support the disposition/termination order.

issues.label: Best-interests factors weighed
issues.why: The court must consider all relevant best-interest factors (safety, bond, stability, permanence, well-being) and explain them.

issues.label: Preponderance best-interests met
issues.why: The court must find termination is more likely than not in JS’s best interests, not merely permissible.

issues.label: Separate analysis from grounds
issues.why: The court must not conflate statutory grounds with best interests; it must make an independent best-interests determination.

issues.label: Written order accuracy
issues.why: The termination order must accurately reflect the grounds, findings, and legal standards applied.

issues.label: Appellate review preservation
issues.why: The court must create a record sufficient for review, including exhibits, rulings, and factual findings.
